questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Horizon at the level of the eye
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of an eye-level horizon on the viewer
questions.stem: A transit planner proposes a mural for the new concourse in which the horizon line runs at the height of a standing viewer's eye rather than at the far end of the concourse. What effect does this choice produce?

options.text: The horizon sits at the viewer's own eye level, so the painted scene reads as an extension of the concourse.
The horizon rises high in the panel, lifting the far distance well above the viewer's own level.
options.misconception: treats a low horizon as evidence the scene is seen from above

options.text: The horizon drops low in the panel, so the whole scene seems to be viewed from high above the floor.
options.misconception: confuses a raised horizon with a high viewpoint

options.text: The horizon becomes a fixed measurement, so the mural can be fitted to the wall's dimensions exactly.
options.misconception: believes horizon height is a practical measurement constraint

questions.explanation: A horizon at eye level lets the painted world continue the real one, so the viewer seems to stand inside it. A high or low horizon instead implies a raised or lowered vantage point.
questions.hint: Ask where the viewer's own eye meets the painted scene.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Compute the retained fraction of a foreshortened length
questions.stem: The board's plan for the concourse records that a handrail running directly away from the viewer is drawn 4.0 metres long at the near end and 1.0 metre long at the far end, while the same rail crossing the view stays 4.0 metres throughout. What fraction of the near drawn length is the far drawn length?

options.text: One quarter, since 1.0 divided by 4.0 gives 0.25 of the near drawn length.
Three quarters, since the drawn length falls from 4.0 to 1.0, a drop of 3.0 metres.
options.misconception: reports the amount lost as though it were the amount kept

options.text: One half, since the far section is half as long as the near section of the rail.
options.misconception: halves the drawn length without using the recorded numbers

options.text: One fifth, since the near rail loses half a metre for every metre it recedes.
options.misconception: invents a rate of loss rather than comparing the two ends

questions.explanation: The far section is drawn at 1.0 metre against a near section of 4.0 metres, so it keeps one part in four of the near length. A rail crossing the view keeps its full length because nothing is compressed.
questions.hint: Compare the far drawn length with the near drawn length.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Depth without a vanishing point
questions.learningObjective: Explain how depth is built without converging lines
questions.stem: A planner asks why a painted panel of a crowded market square can show figures standing one behind another at believable depths even though no lines converge to a single point anywhere in the picture. Explain how depth is produced instead.

answer.exemplar: Depth is created by stacking overlapping figures in receding tiers, by making those figures smaller as they recede, by raising them in the picture field, and by shifting their feet upward and heads downward toward the upper zone, so that each tier reads as further away without any converging construction lines.

questions.explanation: Without a vanishing point, depth comes from overlapping tiers, reduced size and vertical displacement up the panel. Each device tells the eye that a nearer object overlaps and blocks a further one.
questions.hint: Think about overlap, size and vertical placement.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the ratio between figures of different rank
questions.stem: A transit board panel shows a duke 3.0 metres tall beside an attendant 1.5 metres tall. Express the duke's height as a multiple of the attendant's height, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The duke measures 3.0 metres and the attendant 1.5 metres, so the ratio is 3.0 divided by 1.5, which equals exactly 2. The gap in size is a statement of rank, not a record of perspective.
questions.hint: Divide the taller figure's height by the shorter one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bands or registers
questions.learningObjective: Read the function of stacked horizontal registers

stimulus.body: Minutes of the concourse art panel note that the concourse frieze is organised as a horizontal band running the full length of the wall, divided by painted lines into stacked rows of figures, each row carrying one rank of people.

questions.stem: According to the minute, what is the structural purpose of dividing the concourse frieze into stacked horizontal rows of figures?

options.text: The rows let the artist place groups of increasing importance at distinct heights, so rank is legible without labels.
The rows disguise the uneven ground of the wall by covering it with regular divisions.
options.misconception: reads the divisions as decorative cover rather than ordering

options.text: The rows increase the number of figures the artist can fit on a narrow wall.
options.misconception: assumes the bands exist mainly to fit more figures in

options.text: The rows reproduce the physical tiers of seating in the new concourse.
options.misconception: takes the register device as a literal copy of the seating

questions.explanation: The minute assigns one rank of people to each row, so the device is an ordering system that makes social position readable at a glance. Nothing in the minute suggests decoration, capacity or a copy of seating.
questions.hint: Notice what each row is said to carry.

questions.topic: Profile head with a frontal eye
questions.learningObjective: Identify and explain the profile head with a frontal eye
questions.stem: A carved head on a concourse pier is shown in profile, yet the eye is carved fully round and frontal, looking straight out at the viewer. First identify the convention being used; then state what the artist gains from it.

options.text: A profile head with a frontal eye, so the eye stays legible while the head still shows its side.
A twisted three-quarter view, used to suggest the head is turning toward the viewer during the viewing.
options.misconception: reads the turned eye as a rotating three-quarter view

options.text: An optical correction of the sculptor's error, used to give the head a livelier expression.
options.misconception: assumes the mismatch is a careless slip by the sculptor

options.text: A frontal head mistakenly placed on a profile body, used to show the figure in a hurry.
options.misconception: takes the combination as a botched placement of the head

questions.explanation: The head follows one convention for the outline and another for the eye, which is a deliberate pairing rather than a mistake. The frontal eye keeps the gaze available from anywhere on the walkway.
questions.hint: Ask whether the head turns or the eye alone does.

questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a gold background signifies
questions.stem: The board has approved a gold background for a new panel showing a seated saint in a plain chapel. What does the gold ground do that a painted landscape background would not?

options.text: It removes the figures from any ordinary place and time, presenting them in a timeless radiant space.
It suggests the panel records an outdoor scene lit by late afternoon sunlight from the west.
options.misconception: reads the gold as a naturalistic source of sunlight

options.text: It increases the apparent depth of the panel by opening a window onto a distant valley.
options.misconception: treats the flat gold as an illusion of deep landscape space

options.text: It shows that the panel belongs to a series illustrating the seasons of the agricultural year.
options.misconception: interprets the background as a reference to seasonal cycles

questions.explanation: A gold ground denies any ordinary setting, and the even shine of metal admits no particular hour or weather. A landscape background does the opposite, placing the figure firmly in a described place.
questions.hint: Ask whether the gold describes a place or refuses to.

questions.topic: Horizon at the level of the eye
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of a canvas lying below a horizon
questions.stem: The board's elevation survey of the concourse wall records that a mural canvas 120 centimetres high has its horizon line 96 centimetres above the lower edge. What fraction of the canvas height lies below the horizon line?

options.text: Four fifths, since 96 divided by 120 gives 0.8 of the canvas height.
One fifth, since 120 minus 96 gives 24 and 24 over 120 is 0.2.
options.misconception: answers with the share above the line instead of below

options.text: A little over one half, since the horizon looks near the middle of the panel in the drawing.
options.misconception: judges the position by eye rather than by measurement

options.text: Nine tenths, since the horizon sits 24 centimetres below the top edge of 120.
options.misconception: measures down from the top instead of up from the bottom

questions.explanation: The band below the horizon is 96 centimetres of a canvas 120 centimetres tall, which is 0.8 or four fifths of the height. The remaining fifth is the open zone above the line.
questions.hint: Measure up from the lower edge and divide by the whole height.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Explain the cause and effect of foreshortening
questions.stem: A board member asks how a figure seen at an angle can look shorter on the wall than the same figure seen straight on, without the artist simply drawing a different person. Explain what foreshortening is and why it happens.

answer.exemplar: Foreshortening is the compression of a form along the line of sight. A body tilted towards the viewer is seen along its length, so the part nearest the eye is large and the far part is squeezed into a narrow band, and the whole figure appears shorter. The shortening records how the object meets the eye, not a change in the object's real size.

questions.explanation: When a form points towards the viewer, its length is seen end-on and is compressed on the surface. Nothing about the object has changed; only the angle between it and the eye has.
questions.hint: Think about a rod held with one end towards you.

questions.stem: In a painted hall built without a vanishing point, the painter stacks four receding rows of figures whose heights on the panel are 24, 18, 14 and 10 centimetres. What is the total height in centimetres occupied by the four rows?
questions.explanation: Adding the four row heights gives 24 plus 18, which is 42, and 14 plus 10, which is 24, and 42 plus 24 is 66 centimetres. The shrinking rows are a way of stacking depth without any converging construction lines.
questions.hint: Add the four heights in two pairs, then combine the pairs.

questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish rank scale from depth scale

stimulus.body: The minute for the ticket hall mural notes that the magistrate is drawn at twice the height of the porter beside him, that both stand on the same painted ground line, and that no attempt has been made to draw the space between them in perspective.

questions.stem: On the board's own account, what does the doubled height of the magistrate against the porter signify?

options.text: It states that the magistrate outranks the porter, and does not place the magistrate nearer the viewer.
It shows that the magistrate was drawn from life and the porter taken from a quick sketch.
options.misconception: attributes the size difference to copying practice

options.text: It compensates for the mural being viewed by seated passengers from below the scene.
options.misconception: reads the scale as a correction for the viewing angle

options.text: It records that the two figures were painted by different hands working in different styles.
options.misconception: blames the size difference on inconsistent workmanship

questions.explanation: Because both figures stand on one ground line and the space between them is not rendered in perspective, the difference of size can only be doing the work of rank. The minute offers no support for copying, viewing angle or workmanship.
questions.hint: Note what the minute says about the ground line and perspective.

questions.stem: The concourse frieze is divided into three stacked horizontal bands, each holding one rank of figures. First say how the stacking orders the people shown, then say what the arrangement does not imply.

options.text: The stacking orders the crowd by status, and it does not place anyone further back in space.
The stacking records the order in which the frieze was painted, and it does not indicate the standing of anyone shown.
options.misconception: misreads registers as a record of the working schedule

options.text: The stacking shows the crowd walking in procession, and it does not separate them into ranks at all.
options.misconception: confuses horizontal bands with a sequential procession

options.text: The stacking fills the wall efficiently, and it does not convey any hierarchy of the figures.
options.misconception: treats the device as mere filling space with no meaning

questions.explanation: Each band holds one rank, so the order of the bands is an order of status. Because every figure in a band stands on the same line, the device places nobody in a deeper space.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Profile head with a frontal eye
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reason for combining profile and frontal eye
questions.stem: A stone head on the ticket hall pier is carved in profile yet the eye is left fully round. Which explanation fits this combination best?

options.text: The sculptor keeps the profile clear for the outline while the frontal eye meets the viewer directly.
The sculptor was working from a damaged block that left the eye in its natural round state.
options.misconception: explains the combination as damage or accident

options.text: The head is intended to be read as turning slowly as the viewer walks past along the pier.
options.misconception: reads the fixed gaze as an illusion of movement

options.text: The eye was carved first and the profile cut around it in a noticeably different style.
options.misconception: invents two separate carving campaigns for the head

questions.explanation: The pairing is a convention with a purpose: the profile gives a legible silhouette and the round eye gives a gaze the viewer can meet. Damage or a rotation effect would not explain the deliberate combination of both.
questions.hint: Ask what each part of the head is doing separately.

questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: Compute the intact share of a gilded surface
questions.stem: The conservation note for the ticket hall panel records that of 200 square centimetres of gilding on the background, 150 square centimetres are still bright and 50 are dulled where handling has worn the leaf. What percentage of the gilding area is still bright?

options.text: Seventy-five per cent, since 150 divided by 200 gives 0.75 of the gilded area.
Twenty-five per cent, since the worn 50 square centimetres are taken as the bright share.
options.misconception: reports the damaged share instead of the intact share

options.text: Seventy per cent, since the total gilded area has been rounded up from 200 to 215.
options.misconception: divides by an inflated estimate of the gilded area

options.text: Eighty per cent, since the dulled area is subtracted from the bright count a second time.
options.misconception: subtracts the worn area from the bright figure as well

questions.explanation: Half of the gilded area would be 100 square centimetres, and the bright area of 150 is three quarters of the whole. The remaining quarter is the dulled part described in the note.
questions.hint: Divide the bright area by the total gilded area.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Horizon at the level of the eye
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a level horizon extends the real space
questions.stem: A planner asks why the horizon in the concourse mural is not drawn where the far wall of the real concourse meets the floor. Explain what a level horizon at eye height does for the viewer.

answer.exemplar: A horizon drawn at eye height meets the eye exactly where the real room would, so the viewer cannot tell where the painted space stops and the concourse begins. This extends the real building into the picture and makes the viewer feel placed inside the scene rather than outside it looking in, which is why the horizon is held at a standing person's eye level.

questions.explanation: The eye-level horizon makes the painted ground meet the viewer's own sight, so the concourse seems to continue into the panel. Placing the horizon at the far wall's base would instead advertise the panel as a flat object.
questions.hint: Compare the line with the viewer's own eye height.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Apply the right-angled triangle to a leaning ladder
questions.stem: A planning sketch shows a 6 metre ladder leaning against a wall with its foot 4.8 metres out from the base of the wall. How high up the wall, in metres, does the top of the ladder reach?
questions.explanation: The ladder, the wall and the floor form a right triangle, so the height is the square root of 6 squared minus 4.8 squared, that is 36 minus 23.04, giving 12.96 and a height of 3.6 metres.
questions.hint: Use Pythagoras on the ladder, the wall and the floor.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Depth without a vanishing point
questions.learningObjective: Recognise tiered depth in a non-perspectival panel

stimulus.body: The minute for the ticket hall mural states that no point on the wall has been marked as the place from which lines converge. Instead the painter has arranged figures in overlapping tiers, each tier smaller and higher in the panel than the one before it, so that a crowd of many depths fills the surface.

questions.stem: According to the minute, how is depth achieved in the ticket hall mural?

options.text: By stacked overlapping tiers of shrinking figures, without any converging construction lines.
By converging construction lines that were removed after the painting had been finished.
options.misconception: assumes a vanishing point was painted and then cut away

options.text: By careful aerial perspective applied only to the figures standing furthest away.
options.misconception: credits the depth to colour fading rather than to tiering

options.text: By the many columns that frame the scene on both sides of the mural.
options.misconception: attributes the depth to framing columns rather than figure tiers

questions.explanation: The minute states explicitly that no convergence point was marked and that the tiers do the work instead. Aerial perspective and framing columns are not mentioned and would not explain a crowd of many depths.
questions.hint: Read what the minute says was and was not marked.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: State what a size difference asserts and denies
questions.stem: In the concourse mural the head gardener is drawn at 54 centimetres and the boy gardener at 27 centimetres, both on one ground line. First identify what the size difference is doing, then say what it cannot be telling us.

options.text: It asserts that the head gardener outranks the boy, and it cannot be reporting their true heights.
It asserts that the head gardener is nearer the viewer, and it cannot be saying anything about rank.
options.misconception: reads hierarchy as mere proximity and denies rank

options.text: It asserts that the head gardener was twice as tall in life, and it cannot be a claim of importance.
options.misconception: treats the scale difference as literal measurement only

options.text: It asserts that the boy stands on a lower step, and it cannot be a claim of rank at all.
options.misconception: substitutes a physical step for the statement of status

questions.explanation: A doubled figure on a shared ground line is the classic signal of hierarchy, and nothing in the drawing can establish a literal stature. Treating the ratio as distance or as a step would misuse the device.
questions.hint: Ask what a doubled figure on one line normally signals.

questions.topic: Bands or registers
questions.learningObjective: Explain why artists stack figures in horizontal rows
questions.stem: Why do fresco painters sometimes stack figures in horizontal rows rather than scatter them across the surface?

options.text: Rows let the painter sort groups by importance and show many people within a limited height.
Rows are used because fresh fresco plaster cannot hold figures placed at irregular heights.
options.misconception: gives a technical material reason for the arrangement

options.text: Rows let the painter show the crowd walking forward across the surface of the wall.
options.misconception: confuses stacked rows with a continuous narrative scene

options.text: Rows allow the painter to avoid drawing a ground line at the base of the composition.
options.misconception: assumes rows exist to dispense with a ground line

questions.explanation: Rows give the painter a way to show a large number of people and to order them by importance within a narrow height. They do not depict movement, and plaster is not the reason for the convention.
questions.hint: Ask what a row lets the painter say about its contents.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a gold ground is not a literal sky
questions.stem: A board member asks why the chapel panel's gold background should not be understood as a picture of a golden sky. Explain what the gold ground signifies and why it is not a literal landscape.

answer.exemplar: The gold ground is not a sky or a room but a sign that the scene is removed from ordinary time and place, presenting the figure in a heavenly, unchanging realm. Its even, shadowless shine denies the ordinary light of a specific hour, and the punched and incised decoration that catches the light treats gold as a precious material in its own right.

questions.explanation: A gold field has no horizon, no weather and no light source, so it cannot be a described sky. Its purpose is to remove the scene from ordinary place and time and to signal a precious, timeless realm.
questions.hint: Ask whether the gold tells you where or when the scene is.

questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Recognise foreshortening in a reclining figure

stimulus.body: The scene painter's report for the concourse mural records that a reclining figure shown on a bench is drawn with the far shoulder and far knee much smaller than the near ones, so that the figure seems to stretch away from the viewer across the seat rather than lie flat across the panel.

questions.stem: On the painter's own account, why is the reclining figure drawn with its far shoulder and knee smaller?

options.text: The figure is foreshortened, so the part of it running away from the viewer is drawn compressed.
The figure is drawn small because the painter needed room for the passengers standing behind it.
options.misconception: explains the compression as a practical shortage of space

options.text: The figure is drawn small because it belongs to a more distant group of travellers.
options.misconception: misreads a single foreshortened figure as part of a distant group

options.text: The figure is drawn small because the bench itself was drawn with a sloping top.
options.misconception: blames the bench shape rather than the angle of the figure

questions.explanation: The report describes a figure lying with its length running away from the viewer, which is exactly the condition for foreshortening. A shortage of space or a sloping bench would affect the whole group, not one figure's far end.
questions.hint: Look at which parts of the figure are reduced.

questions.learningObjective: Name and read the depth device in a tiered scene
questions.stem: A market scene is painted with no point of convergence, and the painter stacks the crowd in receding tiers of shrinking figures. First name the depth device in use, then say how the viewer reads the order of the tiers.

options.text: Overlapping tiers, and the viewer reads the order from the large low figures to the small high ones.
Aerial perspective, and the viewer reads the order from the cooler colours to the warmer ones.
options.misconception: credits the depth to colour alone and misstates the device

options.text: Measured perspective, and the viewer reads the order from the cast shadows falling on the ground.
options.misconception: claims a measured system that the panel does not use

options.text: Overlapping tiers, and the viewer reads the order only from the written names beside each group.
options.misconception: relies on written labels rather than on the painted order

questions.explanation: Stacking smaller figures higher in the panel is the tiered depth device, and the order is read from the large, low figures forward to the small, high ones behind. Colour, shadows and labels are not part of the arrangement described.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of each figure the eye is given.

questions.stem: In the concourse mural a magistrate is drawn twice the height of the porter standing beside him, even though both stand on the same ground line. What is the primary meaning of this difference in scale?

It is a technical aid to perspective, placing the magistrate nearer to the viewer.
options.misconception: reads hierarchical scale as an optical perspective device

questions.explanation: Two figures on one ground line with a deliberate size ratio is the standard signal of rank in panel painting. Perspective, real stature and a raised step would each require evidence the drawing does not supply.

questions.topic: Bands or registers
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the wall space left by stacked bands
questions.stem: The board's elevation of the concourse frieze records three horizontal bands: an upper band 20 centimetres high with seated figures, a middle band 30 centimetres high with standing figures, and a lower band 40 centimetres high with kneeling workers. options.text: None at all, because 20 plus 30 plus 40 already uses the full 90 centimetres.
Ten centimetres, because the three bands together occupy only 80 centimetres.

options.text: Twenty centimetres, because only the two lowest bands need to be counted.
options.misconception: omits the top band from the total of occupied height

options.misconception: counts the top band as if it lay outside the wall

questions.explanation: The three bands total 20 plus 30 plus 40, which is exactly 90 centimetres, the whole of the available section. There is therefore nothing left above them for a fillet.
questions.hint: Add the three band heights before subtracting.

questions.topic: Profile head with a frontal eye
questions.learningObjective: Explain the benefit of combining profile and frontal eye
questions.stem: A visitor notes that the pier carving shows the nose in profile but the eye looking straight out. Explain why an artist would combine these two views in one head.

answer.exemplar: The combination lets the sculptor show the head clearly in profile, which makes its outline and the arrangement of the features legible at a distance, while the rounded frontal eye creates a living gaze directed at the person standing before it. The two conventions are deliberately combined so that the figure reads both as a distinctive individual and as someone who meets the viewer.

questions.explanation: The profile supplies a clear, readable silhouette while the frontal eye supplies a living address to the viewer. Neither element alone does both jobs, which is why the convention combines them.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two views contributes on its own.

questions.hint: Remove the border from both sides, then square the result.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Horizon at the level of the eye
questions.learningObjective: Compare a painted horizon with a viewer's eye height

stimulus.body: The minute for the concourse mural records that the horizon line has been painted at a height of 1.60 metres above the concourse floor, that the standing height of the average passenger is 1.70 metres, and that the painter has been asked to check the line against the eye level of a person standing in the centre of the hall.

questions.stem: Given the measurements in the minute, how does the painted horizon relate to the passengers' own eye level?

options.text: It stands slightly below the passengers' eye level, so it reads as a raised, downward view of the scene.
It matches the passengers' eye level, so the viewer seems to stand inside the painted hall.
options.misconception: confuses standing height with the height of the eye

options.text: It is far above the passengers' heads, so it must record a ceiling rather than a ground line.
options.misconception: treats a low horizon as evidence of a ceiling line

options.text: It has no measurable height because it is painted on a curved wall.
options.misconception: claims the setting makes the measurement impossible

questions.explanation: A standing passenger of 1.70 metres has an eye level near 1.60 metres, which is where the line has been placed, and a line at eye level still reads as slightly low against the full standing height. The result is a level or slightly raised viewpoint, not a match with the whole body.
questions.hint: Compare the painted height with the height of an eye, not of a head.

questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Read the direction of recession from a foreshortened edge
questions.stem: A bench in the concourse mural is drawn with its near edge 60 centimetres long and its far edge 36 centimetres long. First name what the painter has done to the bench, then say which end is running away from the viewer.

options.text: The bench is foreshortened, and the shortening shows the far end running away from the viewer.
The bench is foreshortened, and the shortening shows the near end running away from the viewer.
options.misconception: reverses which end of the bench is the receding one

options.text: The bench has been narrowed for reasons of composition, and the shortening shows no direction at all.
options.misconception: denies that the shape records any direction of recession

options.text: The bench is drawn in profile, and the shortening shows the bench seen from the side.
options.misconception: confuses foreshortening with a flat side view

questions.explanation: A drawn edge that grows shorter along its length is a foreshortened edge, and the shortening always happens at the end running away from the eye. The near edge is the longer one here, so the bench recedes away from the viewer.
questions.hint: Ask which end is drawn shorter and why.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Depth without a vanishing point
questions.learningObjective: List the devices that create depth without a vanishing point
questions.stem: How does a painter create depth in a crowded scene that is built without any converging construction lines?

options.text: By overlapping figures, reducing their size as they recede, and lifting them up the picture surface.
By darkening every distant figure with a wash of grey, whatever its actual distance.
options.misconception: assumes distance is signalled only by darkening

options.text: By drawing the frontmost figures in a slightly blurred hand to suggest that they are moving.
options.misconception: confuses a painter's handling with a signal of depth

options.text: By leaving a wide empty margin around the edges of the painted scene.
options.misconception: believes empty margins themselves create the illusion

questions.explanation: Overlap, reduction in size and upward displacement are the three stacked devices that order figures in depth without any point of convergence. Blurring and empty margins do not place one figure behind another.
questions.hint: Ask how a nearer figure tells the eye it is in front.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the scaling factor between ranked figures
questions.stem: The board's inventory notes that in one wall panel a judge is painted 90 centimetres tall, a clerk 45 centimetres tall and a bearer 15 centimetres tall, all on one ground line. If the panel were redrawn so that the bearer stood at the judge's head height, by what factor would the bearer need to be enlarged?

options.text: Six times, since 90 divided by 15 gives a factor of six to reach the judge's height.
Three times, since the clerk is 45 and the bearer 15, which is a factor of three.
options.misconception: uses the neighbouring clerk rather than the judge as reference

options.text: Two times, since the judge is twice the height of the clerk.
options.misconception: takes the clerk and judge comparison as the required scaling

options.text: Thirty times, since the three heights have been added rather than divided.
options.misconception: adds the figures together instead of forming a ratio

questions.explanation: To reach the judge's 90 centimetres the bearer at 15 centimetres must be multiplied by 90 over 15, which is 6. The graded heights of judge, clerk and bearer are a ranking of importance, not of distance.
questions.hint: Divide the target height by the height to be changed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bands or registers
questions.learningObjective: Explain why stacked bands keep a crowded scene legible
questions.stem: A visitor asks how stacked bands can hold a large number of people in a limited space without the picture becoming confusing. Explain why the device works on a viewer.

answer.exemplar: Each band has its own ground line and its own group, so a viewer reads the surface as a series of stacked shelves rather than as one crowded floor. Because every band holds a single rank and is separated by a clear line, the eye can move from band to band without losing track of which figures belong together, and the picture can hold many people while still staying legible.

questions.explanation: Bands separate a crowd into readable shelves, each with its own group and ground line. That division is what allows many figures to be shown without the viewer losing track of who belongs where.
questions.hint: Think about how the eye moves from one band to the next.

questions.explanation: The distance from the chin to the eye is 24 centimetres of a 30 centimetre head, so 24 over 30 is 0.8, which is 80 per cent. The remaining fifth of the head stands above the eye line.
questions.hint: Divide the distance below the eye by the whole height.

questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: Identify the signs that a background is a gold ground

stimulus.body: The conservation note on the ticket hall panel records that the background is covered with gold leaf laid over red bole, that the surface is punched with a repeating pattern of small circles, and that the panel shows no sky, no architecture and no cast shadow anywhere behind the seated figure.

questions.stem: On the evidence of the conservation note, how should the background of the ticket hall panel be understood?

options.text: As a precious, timeless field, since there is no landscape, no shadow and the surface is punched.
As a diagram of the stars as they appeared above the site of the concourse.
options.misconception: reads the punched decoration as a literal star chart

options.text: As a brick wall, since the red bole shows through beneath the gilding.
options.misconception: mistakes the underlying bole for the visible surface

options.text: As a panel intended for outdoor viewing in bright daylight, since no shadow is cast.
options.misconception: infers an outdoor viewing condition from missing shadows

questions.explanation: The absence of sky, architecture and cast shadow, combined with a punched gold surface, is the standard evidence for a gold ground rather than a described setting. The bole is a preparation layer and is not what the viewer sees.
questions.hint: Weigh up what is absent from the note as well as what is present.

questions.stem: The concourse mural shows a paved square stretching away to a line of buildings. The artist has set the horizon at the level of the standing passenger's eye. First say where the painted horizon falls, then say what it invites the viewer to do.

It falls at the foot of the buildings and invites the viewer to judge the scene from a bird's-eye view.
options.misconception: confuses the eye-level line with a high overlook of the scene

options.text: It falls at eye level and invites the viewer to measure the width of the square with a tape.
options.misconception: treats the effect as a practical measuring instruction

options.misconception: misplaces the horizon below the ground plane entirely

questions.explanation: A horizon at the standing passenger's eye sits on the line of sight and makes the painted square feel continuous with the real one. It is an invitation to occupy the space, not to stand back and inspect a flat panel.

questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a figure's legs may appear shorter
questions.stem: A figure in the ticket hall mural appears to have very short legs although the painter states the same body was used for a standing figure elsewhere. What accounts for the shortened legs?

options.text: The legs point away from the viewer, so foreshortening compresses them rather than making them short.
The legs were cut short by an error in the underdrawing that was never corrected on the wall.
options.misconception: assumes a drawing error rather than an optical effect

options.text: The figure is shown crouching, so the shortened legs record a bent pose rather than foreshortening.
options.misconception: takes foreshortening for a crouching posture

options.text: The legs are hidden behind the hem of the figure's long coat in the drawing as it stands.
options.misconception: invents drapery to account for the missing leg length

questions.explanation: A body pointing away from the eye is seen along its length and is compressed on the surface, which is why the same figure can look long in one view and short in another. The painter's statement of a shared body rules out an error.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Depth without a vanishing point
questions.learningObjective: Add the measured heights of receding tiers
questions.stem: The board's study of the market panel records that figures in the nearest tier are painted 40 centimetres tall, those in the second tier 30, in the third 22 and in the fourth 16. What is the total height in centimetres of the four tiers when added together?

options.text: One hundred and eight centimetres, since 40 plus 30 plus 22 plus 16 comes to 108.
One hundred and twelve centimetres, since the four figures are simply added as drawn.
options.misconception: adds an extra allowance to the sum of the tiers

options.text: Seventy-six centimetres, since only the three smaller tiers are counted.
options.misconception: leaves the nearest tier out of the sum

options.text: Ninety-six centimetres, since the largest tier is counted twice by mistake.
options.misconception: double counts the largest tier instead of adding it once

questions.explanation: Adding the four tier heights in pairs gives 40 plus 30, which is 70, and 22 plus 16, which is 38, and 70 plus 38 is 108 centimetres. The shrinking heights are what place the tiers in order behind one another.
questions.hint: Add the four heights in two pairs before combining them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: Explain how scale carries meaning without a label
questions.stem: A visitor asks why the giant figure on the ticket hall wall is painted many times the size of the figures on the bench below. Explain how a painter signals importance through size without using any written label.

answer.exemplar: The painter enlarges the important figure far beyond the natural scale of the figures beside it, while the lesser figures are kept small or reduced. Because both stand on a shared ground line and keep the same bodily proportions, the viewer reads the difference as rank and significance rather than as distance, and the meaning is carried entirely by scale.

questions.explanation: Because the bodies stay in proportion and the ground line is shared, the viewer cannot read the size gap as distance, so it is read as importance. That makes scale a carrier of meaning without any inscription.

questions.topic: Profile head with a frontal eye
questions.learningObjective: Read the reasoning behind a freed frontal eye

stimulus.body: The sculptor's report for the pier head states that the skull, nose and mouth are carved to be seen from the side, that the eye has been turned out of the profile plane and left round so that it can be met from any point on the walkway, and that the same treatment is used on the four heads flanking the stair.

Because the sculptor had no time left to model the eye fully before the pier was finished.
options.misconception: explains the treatment as carelessness under time pressure

options.text: So that the head can appear to turn continuously as the viewer walks up the stair.
options.misconception: misreads a fixed frontal gaze as an illusion of turning

options.misconception: attributes the convention to the curve of the support

questions.explanation: The report gives the reason directly: the round eye can be met from any position on the walkway while the head stays in profile. Time pressure and a curve in the pier would not explain the deliberate repetition on all four heads.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: State the meaning and the spatial effect of a gold ground
questions.stem: A new panel for the ticket hall shows a seated saint on a flat gold field. First say what the gold ground does to the figure's place in the world, then say what it does to the sense of distance behind the figure.

It sets the figure in a domestic interior, and it opens a deep landscape behind the figure.
options.misconception: treats the gold as an interior and grants it depth

options.text: It places the figure in a crowded street, and it gives the background a measurable depth.
options.misconception: confuses the timeless field with an everyday street scene

options.misconception: reads the flat field as a landscape with a hidden horizon

questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Compute the fraction of length lost to foreshortening
questions.stem: A sightline study on the board notes that a handrail seen almost end-on shows 5 metres of real length as 4 metres of apparent length, while a walkway crossing the concourse diagonally shows 15 metres on the plan but 12 metres to the eye. What fraction of the real length of the leaning sign post is lost to foreshortening?

options.text: One fifth, since 5 minus 4 equals 1, and 1 over 5 is a fifth of the length.
One quarter, since the apparent 4 metres is a quarter short of the true 5 metres.
options.misconception: misreads a fifth of the length as a quarter of it

options.text: Two fifths, since the apparent 4 metres is two fifths of the true length.
options.misconception: confuses the fraction retained with the fraction lost

options.text: Three fifths, since the loss of 1 metre is three fifths of the apparent length.
options.misconception: measures the loss against the shortened length instead

questions.explanation: The apparent length of 4 metres is 1 metre short of the true 5, and 1 over 5 is one fifth of the real length. The walkway figure shows the same principle for a longer object seen at an angle.
questions.hint: Find the difference, then divide by the true length.

questions.topic: Depth without a vanishing point
questions.learningObjective: Describe the devices that order figures in depth
questions.stem: A planner wants the depth order of two figures in a painted hall to be unambiguous for people who cannot see. Explain what devices a painter without converging construction lines would use to make the nearer figure read as nearer.

answer.exemplar: The painter would overlap the further figure with the nearer one so that part of the further body is hidden, draw the nearer figure larger, place the nearer feet lower in the panel while the further feet sit higher, and soften detail and colour on the more distant figure. Together these cues fix the order without a single converging line.

questions.explanation: Without convergence, the eye relies on overlap, size, vertical placement and the handling of detail. Stacking those cues fixes the order of the figures for any viewer, sighted or not.
questions.hint: List the cues that do not need a vanishing point.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a foreshortened body looks smaller
questions.stem: The board has been told that a figure lying down appears smaller than an upright figure of the same size. Explain how that can happen without the artist making the figure smaller in fact.

answer.exemplar: When a body points away from the viewer, the eye receives its length along the line of sight rather than across it, so the far end is compressed into a narrow band. A figure lying down and pointing towards the viewer is therefore foreshortened and appears short, while the same body seen side on appears at full length. The change is in the angle of viewing, not in the size of the thing.

questions.explanation: The apparent size of a form depends on the angle between it and the eye. Seen along its length, a body is compressed; seen across its length, the same body is at full size.
questions.hint: Ask how the eye receives the length of the body.

questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: Interpret graded heights on a shared ground line

stimulus.body: The minute for the wall panel states that the platform manager is painted at 60 centimetres, the station clerk at 40 centimetres and the porter at 20 centimetres, that all three stand on the same line of paving, and that the manager's proportions are as correct as anyone else's.

questions.stem: What do the three heights recorded in the minute communicate?

options.text: They grade the figures by standing, since each is drawn at correct proportion on one shared line.
They place the three figures at three different distances, since size follows distance in the panel.
options.misconception: reads graded scale as a measure of distance rather than rank

options.text: They record the true stature of the three members of station staff.
options.misconception: takes the graded heights as a record of real stature

options.text: They show that the manager is drawn by a less practised hand than the porter.
options.misconception: attributes the size difference to the skill of the painter

questions.explanation: Three correct-proportioned figures standing on one line, at three graded heights, communicate rank and nothing else. Distance would require a ground plane, and true stature is not what a graded scheme records.
questions.hint: Note what the minute says about proportions and the paving line.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bands or registers
questions.learningObjective: Compare stacked bands with a single overlapping crowd
questions.stem: A painted panel stacks three horizontal bands of figures, the highest band holding a seated council. First say what the bands do for the viewer, then say what a single overlapping crowd would fail to give.

options.text: The bands give a clear order of rank, while a single overlapping crowd leaves the viewer unsure of it.
The bands compress the scene into a small space, while a single crowd would give a stronger sense of movement.
options.misconception: describes the practical purpose rather than the meaning of the tiers

options.text: The bands record the building stages of the panel, while a single crowd would show only one stage.
options.misconception: misreads registers as a record of the painting's stages

options.text: The bands separate the figures from one another, while a single crowd would allow them to overlap freely.
options.misconception: reduces the device to a matter of spacing figures apart

questions.explanation: Bands make rank explicit by giving each group its own shelf, whereas an overlapping crowd leaves the hierarchy to be inferred and easily lost. The point of the device is meaning, not economy or spacing.
questions.hint: Ask what the viewer can and cannot tell in each arrangement.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Profile head with a frontal eye
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a profile eye from a round frontal eye
questions.stem: What is the difference between carving an eye in strict profile and carving it round and frontal within a profile head?

options.text: The round frontal eye can meet the viewer's gaze directly, while a profile eye belongs to the head's side view.
The round frontal eye makes the head appear to turn, while a profile eye fixes the head firmly.
options.misconception: confuses a fixed gaze with a turning head

options.text: The two treatments are identical in effect, because the eye is the smallest part of the head.
options.misconception: denies that the two treatments produce different effects

options.text: The round frontal eye shows the head carved from the front, while a profile eye shows it from above.
options.misconception: misidentifies the direction from which each head is seen

questions.explanation: A profile eye is drawn or carved as part of the side view and cannot meet the viewer, while a round frontal eye faces outward whatever angle the head is seen from. The two treatments therefore produce visibly different results.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two can be met by the viewer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: Compute an area from a percentage of a gilded surface
questions.stem: A conservation survey of the ticket hall panel measures the gilded background at 4.5 square metres and finds that the punched pattern covers 60 per cent of that area. How many square metres of the background carry the punched decoration?

options.text: Two point seven square metres, since 4.5 multiplied by 0.6 gives 2.7.
One point eight square metres, since the remaining 40 per cent has been multiplied by 4.5.
options.misconception: multiplies the gilded area by the uncovered share

options.text: Seven point five square metres, since the two percentages have been added to the total.
options.misconception: adds the two percentages before scaling the total

options.text: Nine tenths of a square metre, since 60 per cent has been treated as an area in metres.
options.misconception: treats the percentage figure as an area in square metres

questions.explanation: The punched area is 60 per cent of the gilded field, so 4.5 multiplied by 0.6 gives 2.7 square metres. The remaining 1.8 square metres of gilding is smooth and carries no punched pattern.
questions.hint: Multiply the total gilded area by the punched share.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Horizon at the level of the eye
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequences of holding a horizon at eye level
questions.stem: The board asks why the horizon in the concourse mural is drawn at the eye level of the standing passenger rather than at the top or the bottom of the wall. Explain the consequences for the viewer.

answer.exemplar: An eye-level horizon meets the viewer's own sight, so the painted world continues the real concourse without a visible break. The wall then reads as an opening rather than as a picture hung on a surface, and the figures inside it share the viewer's own upright posture and scale. Drawing the horizon high or low would announce a raised or lowered viewpoint and turn the wall back into an object.

questions.explanation: An eye-level horizon removes the visible edge between wall and world, so the viewer occupies the scene instead of inspecting it. A high or low horizon would instead advertise a viewpoint the viewer does not share.
questions.hint: Consider what the viewer sees of the wall's own surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Foreshortening
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage shortening of a receding edge
questions.stem: A receding floor panel is drawn with the near edge 25 centimetres long and the far edge 15 centimetres long. By what percentage has the drawn far edge shortened relative to the near edge?
questions.explanation: The drawn edge loses 25 minus 15, which is 10 centimetres, and 10 over 25 is 0.4, which is 40 per cent. The shortening is the effect of foreshortening on a surface running away from the viewer.
questions.hint: Find the loss, then divide by the near edge.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Depth without a vanishing point
questions.learningObjective: Identify the depth devices named in a painter's report

stimulus.body: The painter's report on the market panel states that the crowded market is built from tiers of figures that overlap one another, each tier smaller and set higher on the panel than the tier in front, and that no lines have been laid down to mark a place where the view could converge.

questions.stem: What does the painter's report identify as the source of depth in the market panel?

options.text: The tiers alone, since overlap, reduced scale and upward placement put the figures in order.
The tiers are decorative bands, and the real depth comes from a vanishing point used elsewhere.
options.misconception: credits the depth to a vanishing point the panel does not use

options.text: The tiers give the depth, though the figures within them are drawn with distorted bodies.
options.misconception: adds a claim of distorted bodies that was never made

options.text: The tiers separate the crowd into groups, and each group stands in a different landscape.
options.misconception: invents separate landscapes for the different groups

questions.explanation: The report names exactly three devices, overlap, reduced size and upward placement, and states that no convergence was laid down. Distorted bodies and separate landscapes are nowhere mentioned in it.
questions.hint: Use only what the report actually states.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: State what a size difference asserts and leaves open
questions.stem: On the last panel of the concourse the stationmaster is drawn at twice the height of the porters on either side of him. First say what the drawing asserts, then say what it leaves the viewer to judge for themselves.

options.text: It asserts that the stationmaster holds the greater rank, and it leaves his true stature unstated.
It asserts that the stationmaster stands nearer the viewer, and it leaves his true stature unstated.
options.misconception: swaps the rank meaning for a spatial one

options.text: It asserts that the porters are unusually small men, and it leaves the stationmaster's real height unstated.
options.misconception: turns a rank statement into a claim about the porters' bodies

options.text: It asserts that the stationmaster is raised on a platform, and it leaves his rank unstated.
options.misconception: substitutes a physical platform for a social statement

questions.explanation: A doubled figure on a shared ground line is the standard signal of hierarchy, and the drawing makes no claim about real stature. Reading the ratio as proximity, as small porters or as a raised step all misuse the convention.
questions.hint: Ask which conventional meaning a doubled figure carries.
